messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Margaret's Burden

Margaret Chen had been seventy-three years old for six months when the nursing home collapsed. She had gone to visit her husband Robert on a Tuesday afternoon in March, bringing him the lemon bars he loved, parking in the familiar spot near the east entrance of Riverside Gardens. The building had been constructed in 1987, and the structural engineer's report would later confirm that a combination of deferred maintenance and a structural failure in the north wall had created an invisible catastrophe waiting to happen. Margaret had been in Robert's room on the second floor when she heard the sound—not a crash at first, but a deep, terrible groan, as though the building itself was crying out in pain. The floor tilted. A window shattered. She remembered the exact angle of the afternoon light through the dust, the way Robert's wheelchair tipped, the smell of his cologne mixing with plaster and something acrid she would later learn was electrical fire. She had tried to hold him steady, had felt his hand grip hers with a strength she didn't know he still possessed, and then the wall beside them gave way and he was gone—pulled downward into the collapse—and she was falling too, landing hard on her left side, her hip screaming, unable to move, unable to reach him, listening to the sound of concrete settling and people screaming and the terrible, terrible silence underneath it all.

Robert died in the hospital three days later. Margaret survived with a fractured pelvis and a fractured mind.

In the months that followed, certain things had begun to trigger her in ways she could not control. When her daughter wept during a visit, Margaret would find herself rigid, her throat closing, her own tears coming in a flood she couldn't stop—not because she was sad in that moment, but because crying had become the sound of the building falling, the sound of Robert slipping away. When her granddaughter hugged her, Margaret's body would seize. The pressure of another person's arms around her would send her back to that room, to the moment of impact, her left side suddenly remembering the exact position it had been in when the wall came down. Worst of all was the smell of alcohol—her son-in-law's cologne, a hand sanitizer someone used in the kitchen—because the electrical fire had carried that sharp, burning note, and it meant danger was present, it meant the world was about to collapse again.

Margaret had stopped reading the news after the first week. A story about a building fire in Seattle sent her into a panic that lasted six hours. She had found that if she kept her mind occupied—painting, television, organizing the same cupboard three times a day—she could sometimes push the memories back. But they came anyway, especially at night. She would lie awake listening for sounds, certain that someone was entering her home, that danger was coming. The photographic quality of her memories was almost unbearable: she could see every detail of that afternoon with perfect clarity, could replay it frame by frame, and with each remembering came a crushing weight of guilt. Why had she gone that day? Why hadn't she insisted Robert move to a different facility? Why had she survived when he hadn't?

What frightened Margaret most was the certainty that had settled into her bones: that she would never feel anything normal again, that the world she had believed in—a world where you could visit your husband safely, where buildings stood, where love protected you—was a lie. She had come to believe that her life was no longer worth the effort of living it. She had not said this to her daughter, but she thought it every morning when she woke.

It was her daughter who finally insisted she see someone. Margaret had agreed only because she was tired of fighting, tired of the vigilance, tired of the way her own body had become a stranger to her. She sat in the therapist's office with her hands folded in her lap, wondering if anyone could possibly understand what it meant to have watched your entire world—the person in it, the safety of it, the meaning of it—simply cease to exist.
